analysis.one_liner: Bans meatpackers from buying livestock through opaque formula-priced forward contracts, requiring firm prices and open public bidding.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the House; it sat in the Agriculture Committee and its livestock subcommittee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended a century-old law governing meatpackers to prohibit certain forward contracts — agreements to buy livestock for later delivery at a price not fixed on the day of the deal. It would have required any forward contract to carry a firm base price set on the contract day, be offered through open public bidding that buyers and sellers can witness, and cover only small lots (40 cattle or 30 hogs or fewer). Formula prices, where the final price is calculated later from a market number not yet known, would have been banned. Cooperatives and very small packers were exempted.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers — ranchers and farmers who sell cattle and hogs to meatpackers. Today a packer can sign a forward contract with no firm price, with the final payment calculated later from a formula tied to a market number. Sellers who sign such deals don't know what they'll be paid, and because the contracts aren't bid publicly, buyers don't have to compete openly for the livestock. The bill would have forced packers to name a real price up front and to bid in the open, which tends to raise and stabilize what sellers receive.

how_it_helps.text: It would require every forward contract to contain a firm base price that can be equated to a fixed dollar amount on the day the contract is signed, so sellers know what they are being paid when they commit.
It would require forward contracts to be offered for bid in an open, public manner, where both buyers and sellers can participate in and witness bids, replacing private negotiated deals.

It would ban formula-priced contracts — deals where the purchase price is calculated later from a market number not yet determined or reported — and cap contract lots at 40 cattle or 30 hogs unless the Agriculture Secretary adjusts the limits.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies. The bill would restrict their main tools for securing a steady supply of cattle and hogs on terms negotiated privately, forcing them onto open bids with prices fixed in advance and limiting contract sizes to small lots, with exemptions only for cooperatives and very small packers.

drawbacks.text: The lot-size limits are very small — 40 cattle or 30 hogs — so even mid-sized feeding operations that use forward contracts to lock in prices and manage risk would have lost that tool, not just the largest packers, unless the Secretary adjusted the limits.

Banning formula pricing could reduce flexible price discovery in livestock markets; feeders and packers use formula deals tied to futures or reported markets to share risk, and the bill's exclusion for futures-based and verifiable quality adjustments only partially preserves that.
The exemptions for cooperatives and packers with only one plant or no daily reporting requirement create carve-outs that could route deals around the new rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For sellers, the upside is real: a known price at signing and visible competition for their livestock directly counters practices that have long been criticized for opaque pricing. The main cost falls on packers and on larger producers who lose a hedging tool, and the bill's blanket formula-pricing ban plus its small lot caps are blunt instruments that go beyond the narrowest fix. On balance, the bill aims a genuine pricing-transparency protection at independent producers, though its one-size limits are crude.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its livestock subcommittee on August 10, 2011, and neither ever took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia Lummis introduced the bill on July 25, 2011, with Rep. Marcy Kaptur as its cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day.
On August 10, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, where no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 112th Congress.
The bill never advanced to a full committee markup or a House floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies kept their ability to buy livestock through privately negotiated, formula-priced forward contracts without open bidding, while independent ranchers and farmers who sell to them gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Lummis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Livestock Marketing Fairness Act to ban anti-competitive livestock forward contracts.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor, making it a bipartisan two-member effort.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on August 10, 2011 and held no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members were ever attached to the bill — one Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: Packers would lose the ability to lock in cattle and hogs through private forward contracts without a firm price or open bidding, and could no longer use formula pricing or contract lots larger than 40 cattle or 30 hogs. Their current practices shift pricing risk onto sellers who don't know what they'll be paid.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers (ranchers and hog farmers)
industries.note: Producers would get a fixed price at signing and open, visible bidding for their animals, which tends to raise and stabilize what they are paid. Smaller contract producers who relied on forward contracts to manage risk would also lose some flexibility, so the gain is not universal within the sector.

industries.industry: Livestock cooperatives and small single-plant packers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts farmer-owned cooperatives and packers with only one plant or no daily reporting obligation, letting them keep using forward contracts competitors would be barred from.
